American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine

Alveolar Ventilation Efficiency Assessed via Capnography is Associated with Improved Outcomes in Pediatric Cardiac Arrest

Sutton RM, Bender D, Thakur VS et al. · 2026 Sep 19
Study Type: Prospective multicenter observational cohort study
Key Question: Does capnography-derived airway opening index (AOI) during paediatric CPR correlate with survival and neurological outcomes?
Key Findings:
  • Among 99 cardiac arrest events, event-level AOI ≥0.35 was associated with improved survival to discharge (aRR 1.53, 95% CI 1.03–2.28, p=0.04) and favourable neurological outcome (aRR 1.56, 95% CI 1.01–2.41, p=0.04).
  • Findings remained robust after excluding extracorporeal CPR cases.
  • Post-arrest peak lactate was lower with AOI ≥0.35 (6.0 vs 11.5 mmol/L, p=0.006), despite similar CPR durations.
Clinical Relevance: AOI could serve as a real-time, capnography-based CPR quality metric guiding airway management and ventilation optimisation during paediatric resuscitation, relevant to UK PICU and resuscitation practice standards.
Limitations: Small sample size (99 events) from a non-UK cohort limits generalisability and precludes causal inference regarding AOI and outcome.

American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine

Metered-Dose Liquid Nitrogen Cryospray for Chronic Bronchitis: Results From the Prospective, Sham-Controlled Trial (SPRAY-CB)

Criner GJ, Browning RF, Abu-Hijleh M et al. · 2026 Sep 21
Study Type: Prospective, sham-controlled randomised trial (2:1 allocation)
Key Question: Does bronchoscopic metered cryospray (MCS) treatment improve quality of life and reduce exacerbations in COPD patients with chronic bronchitis compared with sham bronchoscopy plus mucus clearance?
Key Findings:
  • MCS produced significantly greater improvement in SGRQ total score (treatment difference -5.9; 95% CI -11.6 to -0.2; p=0.042) and CAT score (-3.4; 95% CI -5.8 to -1.0; p=0.005) versus control.
  • Severe AECOPD rates were numerically lower with MCS (21.3% vs 26.9%), though overall AECOPD rates were similar (70.6% vs 67.2%).
  • Periprocedural pneumothorax occurred in 3.6% of MCS treatments; 8 deaths overall, none device/procedure-related.
Clinical Relevance: Offers a novel bronchoscopic option for symptomatic chronic bronchitis in COPD, a population with limited device-based therapies within current NHS respiratory pathways, though cost-effectiveness and NICE evaluation would be needed before adoption.
Limitations: Modest sample size and unblinded outcome assessment for exacerbations limit certainty around the modest treatment effect sizes and exacerbation benefit.

American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine

Biologic outcomes in severe asthma patients by smoking status: evidence from SHARP

Caminati M, Charriot J, Bansal AT et al. · 2026 Sep 22
Study Type: Retrospective real-world cohort study (multinational registry analysis)
Key Question: Does smoking status (current/ex-smoker vs never-smoker) affect biologic treatment response in severe asthma, and does this influence prescribing practice across Europe?
Key Findings:
  • Across all groups (never-, ex-, and current-smokers, n=3,876), 1-year biologic therapy improved symptom control (ACT/ACQ), reduced exacerbations, improved AQLQ, and reduced oral corticosteroid use, with no statistically significant difference in magnitude of improvement between groups.
  • Current-smokers were under-represented among biologic recipients (n=141 vs 2,383 never-smokers).
  • 29% of countries reported reluctance to prescribe biologics to current smokers; 59% expressed dissatisfaction with existing guideline recommendations on this issue.
Clinical Relevance: UK severe asthma services should not withhold biologics from smokers on efficacy grounds alone, as real-world data show comparable benefit, though smoking cessation support remains essential and current guidelines may need revision.
Limitations: Retrospective, non-randomised design with potential confounding and selection bias, limiting causal inference; RCTs in smokers are needed to confirm findings.

American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine

Combined results of the TETON-1 and TETON-2 Trials of Inhaled Treprostinil for Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis

Nathan SD, Smith P, Deng C et al. · 2026 Sep 23
Study Type: Combined analysis of two replicate phase 3 RCTs (double-blind, placebo-controlled)
Key Question: Does inhaled treprostinil slow lung function decline and improve clinical outcomes in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)?
Key Findings:
  • FVC decline at 52 weeks was significantly attenuated with treprostinil vs placebo (-45.4 mL vs -161.7 mL; between-group difference 111.8 mL, 95% CI 79.7–144.0, p<0.0001).
  • Treprostinil showed superiority in 5 of 6 secondary endpoints: time to clinical worsening, time to IPF exacerbation, K-BILD quality of life, ppDLCO and ppFVC.
  • Fewer deaths with treprostinil (6.9% vs 9.4%); cough was the most frequent adverse event.
Clinical Relevance: These results, from the largest IPF pharmacotherapy trials to date, position inhaled treprostinil as a potential new disease-modifying option alongside antifibrotics, relevant to future NICE appraisal and UK ILD service commissioning.
Limitations: The abstract does not detail background antifibrotic use, blinding integrity (given cough as a side effect), or long-term safety beyond 52 weeks.

American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine

Association between Airway Mucus Plugs on Computed Tomography and Respiratory Outcomes in Participants with COPD and with Preserved Spirometry: Findings from a Chinese Population

Wu F, Wu F, Xia T et al. · 2026 Sep 25
Study Type: Prospective community-based cohort study
Key Question: Are CT-detected airway mucus plugs associated with future respiratory outcomes in individuals with preserved spirometry and with COPD (including mild/asymptomatic disease)?
Key Findings:
  • In preserved spirometry participants, ≥3 mucus plugs vs none: higher exacerbation risk (RR 1.42, 95%CI 1.11–1.81) and higher risk of developing spirometry-defined COPD (18.2% vs 7.6%; RR 1.71, 95%CI 1.05–2.78), plus faster FEV1/FVC decline.
  • 1–2 mucus plugs also associated with modestly increased exacerbation risk (RR 1.22, 95%CI 1.01–1.48).
  • In COPD (including mild-to-moderate and asymptomatic subgroups), ≥3 mucus plugs predicted greater total and moderate-to-severe exacerbation risk.
Clinical Relevance: Incidental mucus plugging on chest CT may identify pre-COPD/preserved-spirometry patients at risk of disease progression and exacerbations, supporting consideration of mucus plug burden as an early risk stratifier relevant to UK COPD case-finding and CT lung screening pathways.
Limitations: Observational Chinese cohort with potential residual confounding and uncertain generalisability to other ethnic populations and healthcare settings.

American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine

One-year progression of CT emphysema subtypes predict lung function decline: SPIROMICS

Hermann EA, Hoffman EA, Angelini ED et al. · 2026 Sep 25
Study Type: Prospective cohort study (SPIROMICS)
Key Question: Does one-year progression of quantitative CT (QCT) emphysema measures predict subsequent FEV₁ decline in smokers with and without COPD?
Key Findings:
  • In 880 participants, mean FEV₁ decline was -30.4 mL/year (95% CI -34.5, -26.3).
  • Each SD increase in one-year progression of machine-learned emphysema subtypes predicted accelerated FEV₁ decline: combined bronchitic-apical emphysema (CBaE) -4.2 mL/year (95% CI -8.3, -0.2); diffuse emphysema -6.2 mL/year (95% CI -10.7, -1.8).
  • Standard QCT emphysema metrics also predicted decline, but lost significance when modelled alongside CBaE and diffuse emphysema, which remained independent predictors.
Clinical Relevance: These CT-based emphysema subtypes could serve as short-term intermediate endpoints to accelerate COPD trial design and outcome assessment, relevant to UK respiratory research and future NHS-based imaging biomarker adoption.
Limitations: Observational design with QCT-based surrogate endpoints limits causal inference and generalisability to interventional trial settings.

The Role of Regret in Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Candidacy Decision-Making

Rubin J, Jacobs A, Siegal A et al. · 2026 Sep 21
Study Type: Qualitative study (secondary analysis of semi-structured interviews, directed content analysis)
Key Question: Does clinician regret influence VV ECMO candidacy decision-making?
Key Findings:
  • Clinicians favour utility-based reasoning but often cannot apply it consistently due to uncertainty.
  • Both regret of omission (not offering ECMO) and commission (offering ECMO) shape candidacy decisions.
  • Clinicians use identifiable coping strategies to minimise anticipated and past regret, which may partly drive within-centre inconsistency in decisions.
Clinical Relevance: Understanding regret as a hidden driver of ECMO candidacy decisions is relevant to UK ECMO centres seeking to standardise selection criteria and reduce unwarranted variation in resource allocation.
Limitations: Small, international sample (n=24) using retrospective self-report limits generalisability and risks recall/social desirability bias.

Changes in Inhaled Antibiotic Associated lung function outcomes in the CFTR-Modulator Era

Muhlebach MS, She J, LiPuma JJ et al. · 2026 Sep 21
Study Type: Retrospective registry-based cohort study (US CF Foundation Patient Registry, 2011–2019)
Key Question: Does inhaled antibiotic use in people with CF affect infection risk and lung function differently by Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) status, and has this changed across CFTR-modulator eras?
Key Findings:
  • Inhaled antibiotics were associated with increased risk of Aspergillus (HR 1.33, 95% CI 1.26–1.41), Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (HR 1.21, 1.14–1.29), and Achromobacter (HR 1.26, 1.14–1.39), with highest risk in Pa-negative patients.
  • Lung function benefit from inhaled antibiotics was seen only in chronic Pa patients; Pa-negative patients showed lower lung function with treatment.
  • Antibiotic-associated lung function benefit in chronic Pa patients diminished progressively across successive CFTR-modulator eras.
Clinical Relevance: Supports reassessment of chronic inhaled antibiotic prescribing in UK CF centres, particularly de-escalation in Pa-negative patients and modulator-treated populations, given diminishing benefit and rising non-fermenter/fungal infection risk.
Limitations: Observational registry design with potential residual confounding by indication despite inverse probability weighting.
